task: Fix the broken session invalidation after the distributed cache was replaced with a local cache.

candidate_memories.content: Sessions remain valid after logout because the new local cache is per-instance and invalidation does not propagate.
The session store must use the distributed Redis cache for invalidation to propagate across all service instances.
The local cache was introduced as a performance optimization but invalidation was not considered.
The bug manifests when a user logs out on instance A and then makes a request to instance B.
Session 2 note: a support ticket confirmed users can still access protected resources after logging out.
The service is deployed with 6 instances behind a round-robin load balancer.
Session 8 note: the infrastructure team added a Redis cluster for distributed caching.
Old practice: sessions were stored in a single-instance PostgreSQL before Redis was introduced.
The local cache uses an LRU eviction policy with a 5-minute TTL.
Session 3 note: the security team performed a session fixation vulnerability audit.
Old session guide: session invalidation was instantaneous when a single instance served all requests.
Session invalidation must use a distributed store whenever more than one service instance serves requests.
Session 11 note: the performance team measured a 30% latency reduction with the local cache.
Redis is shared with the job queue and the rate limiter; separate key namespaces are used.
Session 6 note: the load balancer was updated to use session-aware sticky routing for the API.
The service supports horizontal scaling up to 20 instances during peak load.
Performance optimizations that change cache scope must be audited for correctness across multiple instances.
Session 9 note: the security team added a session activity audit log for compliance purposes.
Old cache config: the Redis cache was set as the primary session store in the original architecture design.
The session TTL in Redis is 30 minutes with sliding expiration on each authenticated request.
